replies.author: main_account_4_sure
replies.body:
The inherent complexity in these skills is, obviously, not a valid answer. It could be applicable to anything. Cooking is complex to master yet completely different from, I don't know, archery. The fact I even need to explain this baffles me. 

If that is not a rhetoric question or irony, I'm afraid this discussion is short-lived. If you don't understand the difference between code and art you may need to review a lot of things in your life. 

Art is expression, code is utility. The end user does not care whether you coded an app in 2 years or 15 minutes: it just has to work and solve a problem.

Art is subjective. Someone may listen to Mozart and find it crappy. Someone may listen to a terribly composed Ai song and find it good. Both are valid opinions, it's subjective. Different than code, there is no objective right and wrong.

In videogames, art is the "soul" and expression of it. The end user may want to know how that was generated/made/created to judge whether it's valuable or not and, once again, it's subjective: no right or wrong.

In my experience, gamers find it valuable to see something heart-felt and with actual hardwork involved in art. They don't give a crap about code, and it's understandable, since, as I mentioned, the end goal is to simply make something work. No one cares about "beautifully made" code besides crazy programmers.

comments.author: TheiaTowerOfSoul
comments.body:
Here are my thoughts on this survey.

Japan has a unique market, home to the world’s largest adult game industry with legal, dedicated domestic distribution channels. Within this niche, AI art has been widely adopted. These games mostly focus on visuals and storytelling, with fairly fixed gameplay templates, so AI can quickly generate acceptable assets for players.

That said, this survey covers developers across all game genres, not only adult visual novels.

Opinions on AI in Japan are still divided. Overall acceptance is relatively higher, while most pushback comes from artists whose livelihoods are impacted.

My way of judging AI usage boils down to intent: whether there is malice, which I split into intentional and unintentional harm.

Intentional malice: people who only want fast profit, pumping out low-quality games in bulk without caring about quality. They just rely on volume to find buyers. This kind of rushed cash-grab content is widely disliked, much like spam bots, and actively filtered by community automods and moderators.

Unintentional harm: for example, a new developer has a promising idea but lacks experience. Using AI, they finish and release the game quickly. Meanwhile another team, working on a nearly identical concept without AI, loses the race simply because they built everything manually. The AI user means no harm, yet their release undermines years of work from the other team.

Some will side with the slower team and call it unethical; others argue tools are available for everyone, and it is their choice not to use AI. Both sides have reasonable perspectives, and there is no simple right or wrong.

Generally, the community is more forgiving toward people using AI without harmful intent, even if unintended negative consequences happen. Still, job displacement remains the most tangible conflict brought by AI.

To me, AI is a productivity tool, not a creative tool. When AI generates code or art, it does not truly understand what it creates; it only rearranges existing data from its training set. Games are an art form, yet some developers treat games purely as products to make money. That is why many creators are wary of AI.

Many people around me think refusing AI makes me outdated. I have tried using AI for development myself, with poor results. I do not write handwritten code and build everything in Unreal Blueprints. I wasted lots of time trying to follow AI suggestions, only to solve all problems on my own in the end. After careful consideration, I stick to my workflow.

I have hired a newly graduated remote artist for my project for over a year, paying them $800 every month. Instead of spending money on AI tokens, I prefer supporting a real human creator. My project will not make any difference to AI, but this income truly helps this young artist get by.

Maybe one day AI will move beyond being just a copying and acceleration tool and gain universal acceptance. But if that day comes, it will no longer be AI as we know it. It would be closer to something with its own life, no longer built solely to generate profit for its creators.
